vignette:
She is thirty-eight, an African woman who has spent most of her life on the water. Before the trauma, her days begin long before sunrise. She wakes in the dark beside her husband, ties a scarf over her hair, and walks down to the shore with the other fishers, carrying nets that smell of salt and old rope. She is proud of her strength. On the lake, she knows how to read the wind, how to judge the pull of the net, how to sort the catch quickly with cold, practiced hands. Her husband jokes that she is the better fisherman between them, and she laughs easily then. Their life is hard, but familiar.

The event she returns to again and again happens late one afternoon near the end of the rainy season. She and her husband are out on the water together. The sky has looked uncertain all day, but storms are common, and they have stayed out before. She remembers the change first as a feeling in her body, a sudden tightening in her chest as the wind shifts hard and the surface of the lake turns violent. Rain comes in sheets. The boat begins to pitch. They both move quickly, trying to secure the nets, trying to turn back, but everything happens too fast. A wave slams the side of the boat. Her husband loses his footing. She hears herself scream his name as he goes over.

What lives in her now is not one memory but many fragments that come sharp and complete: his hand breaking the surface; the look on his face, startled more than afraid; the useless burn in her arms as she reaches for him; the rain in her eyes; people shouting from somewhere far away. She cannot remember exactly how long he is in the water, only the certainty, in those seconds, that she is watching him die. He is eventually pulled out by men in another boat, coughing and barely conscious. He survives, but in her mind the event never fully becomes a rescue. It remains a moment of helplessness stretched into something endless.

Afterward, everyone tells her she should be grateful. She tells herself the same thing. Her husband is alive. He heals physically. He returns to the lake within weeks, though more cautiously. But she does not return in the same way. At night she lies awake listening to his breathing, sometimes reaching out in the dark to make sure his chest is still rising. If he shifts in his sleep or coughs, she bolts upright before she knows why. When she does sleep, she dreams of water closing over his head. In the dreams she cannot move, or her hands are full of torn net, or she is shouting and no sound comes out. She wakes drenched in sweat, heart hammering, already afraid of the next night.

The lake, once ordinary, becomes charged with danger. She still goes to work because the family depends on it, but she no longer steps into a boat without scanning the sky again and again. A gust of wind can send her back to that afternoon so quickly that she grips the sides of the boat until her fingers ache. If clouds gather, she insists they return at once. Her husband sometimes tells her the weather is fine, but she hears urgency in her own voice and cannot soften it. On bad days she refuses to go out at all and stays onshore mending nets, though even there the slap of water against wood makes her stomach clench.

She does not like being away from her husband now. If he leaves early without waking her, she feels panic before she even opens her eyes fully. She imagines the boat overturned, imagines people running to call her. She tries to phone him repeatedly when he is on the water, then grows angry at herself for sounding foolish. She knows others see her watching him too closely. She sees it in the way relatives tell her, gently at first and then with impatience, that he is strong, that God spared him, that she must stop thinking so much. Their words make her feel alone. She stops trying to explain.

She has become more irritable at home, especially with noise and with small disruptions she once would have ignored. If a basin drops, if children shout suddenly behind her, she startles so violently that she feels shame immediately afterward. She avoids conversations about storms, drownings, or accidents on the lake. When another fisher's boat capsizes months later, she cannot eat for the rest of the day. Her husband notices that she no longer laughs in the easy way she used to. He tells her she is here with him, safe in the present, but she often does not feel present at all.

In quieter moments she speaks about losing something in herself that day. She still wakes before dawn, still smells the nets, still goes where the fish are, but the work that once felt like a rhythm now feels like an argument with fear. She watches the water as if it has intentions. She carries the memory of almost losing her husband into every ordinary moment: when he is late coming home, when rain begins on the roof, when she hears the lake at night. Part of her knows he survived. Another part remains in that storm, reaching toward him, certain she is about to be left behind.
